extracted.intended_audience: students and educators (and general readers) learning about mathematical proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for what constitutes a mathematical proof, common proof techniques, formal/axiomatic definition of proofs, and conventions for writing/readability. Targets learners and practitioners who construct or check proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a mathematical proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical proof (数学的証明) is a sequence of deductions asserting a proposition is true: each step is derived from premises (axioms, theorems, accepted facts) or assumptions by inference rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes that assumptions introduced in a proof must either be proven elsewhere in the proof or be negated (as in proofs by contradiction). It contrasts direct and indirect proofs as intuitive classifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct proof (直接証明)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove a proposition P by proving P directly from premises and accepted facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when one can derive P straightforwardly by applying definitions, theorems, and inference rules to the given hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect proof via equivalent statement (間接証明)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of proving P directly, prove another statement equivalent to P (or transform P into an equivalent form) and prove that statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as an intuitive classification; useful when an equivalent formulation is easier to establish than P itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contrapositive (対偶法)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove P ⇒ Q, prove the logically equivalent contrapositive ¬Q ⇒ ¬P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method leverages logical equivalence of an implication and its contrapositive; useful when ¬Q ⇒ ¬P is simpler to establish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction / reductio ad absurdum (背理法)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove P by assuming ¬P and deriving a contradiction, thereby showing ¬P is false and P must be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article gives the classical example (infinitude of primes) where one assumes a finite list and constructs a number that yields a contradiction. It notes that showing ¬P is false can be done by deriving an explicit contradiction from ¬P.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproof by counterexample (反例)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a universal statement 'for all x, P(x)' is false, provide a single x for which P(x) is false (use the equivalence ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the straightforward method for refuting universally quantified claims: produce an explicit witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case analysis / classification method (転換法)
rubrics_metrics.description: Partition all possible situations into exhaustive cases (P, Q, R, ...), prove implications for each case (e.g., P⇒A, Q⇒B, R⇒C), and deduce the desired result by considering which case holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article sketches using classification of possibilities and using results for each independent case; helpful when the domain naturally splits into disjoint exhaustive scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness / equivalence by uniqueness (同一法)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A ⇒ B holds and B is satisfied by only one object, then B ⇒ A holds (establishing equivalence by uniqueness properties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when an intermediate property characterizes an object uniquely; proving existence plus uniqueness often yields a strong characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeonhole principle (ディリクレの箱入れ原理)
rubrics_metrics.description: If n+1 objects are placed into n boxes, at least one box contains two or more objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a standard combinatorial principle that serves as the basis for many existence arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical induction (数学的帰納法)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a property P(n) for all natural numbers n, show base case P(1) and show P(n) ⇒ P(n+1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as the standard method for propositions about natural numbers; emphasizes the two-step structure (base and inductive step).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence proofs (存在証明)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof that demonstrates that at least one solution or object satisfying given conditions exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existence proofs may be constructive (produce an example) or non-constructive (argue existence indirectly, e.g., by pigeonhole or compactness). The article lists existence proofs as a standard type of argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness proofs (一意性証明)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof that shows that if a solution exists then it is unique (there is at most one).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often paired with existence proofs to fully characterize solutions (existence + uniqueness). Methods include assuming two solutions and proving they must coincide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal/axiomatic definition of proof (公理系と推論規則による定義)
rubrics_metrics.description: In formalization, fix a finite alphabet, form words (formulas), choose a set of propositions as axioms, and specify inference rules. A proof is a finite sequence (P1,...,Pn) where each Pi is either an axiom or derivable from earlier P1,...,Pi-1 by allowed inference rules; then Pn is provable (a theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a mechanical criterion for correctness of proofs and underlies formal proof theory and proof assistants; it distinguishes between informal mathematical proofs and formal derivations in a proof system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventions for writing proofs (記述の習慣)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use clear markers for the start and end of a proof (e.g., 'Proof', '［証明］', 'Q.E.D.', '□'), structure the proof for readability, and explicitly indicate reasons or used theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists common begin markers ('proof','prf.','［証明］','∵' enclosed), end markers ('Q.E.D.','□','■','／証明終わり'), and recommends: put one idea per line, progress from top to bottom, enclose reasons/theorems used in parentheses, group multiple lines with braces or numbered tags and refer back (e.g., '①,②より'). These conventions are taught strictly at elementary/secondary levels to improve readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability: line-by-line flow and explicit justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Write proofs so each line presents a single content and the progression of implications flows clearly from previous lines; annotate each step with the reason or theorem used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice includes enclosing reasons in parentheses, grouping related lines, and tagging steps for later reference; especially important in educational settings to make the logical flow transparent to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalization for mechanical verification
rubrics_metrics.description: By formalizing proofs (defining alphabet, language, axioms, inference rules) proofs can be mechanically checked and treated as mathematical objects studied in proof theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that formalization enables machine-checking of proofs and makes the correctness of proofs independent of author/reader judgment; this is an alternative standard of correctness beyond informal exposition.
